idiom_name: indirect enum with recursive cases + exhaustive switch
implementation_notes: Swift has a construct built for this: indirect enum boxes the recursive cases automatically and switch over the enum is exhaustive without a default, so a new case breaks every evaluator at compile time. It is the shape the Swift book teaches (its ArithmeticExpression example) and the one most packages use; the class/protocol form is only preferred when nodes must be reference types or subclassed.
pitfalls: indirect boxes each recursive case, so a large tree is a heap pointer graph and ARC traffic dominates evaluation cost; sharing subtrees needs a class wrapper or an index-based arena.
Enums you own cannot be extended by clients: a new grammar rule is a source-breaking change for everyone who switch-matches, which is the point of the exhaustiveness guarantee.
Exhaustive switch plus enums means a default case would sabotage the guarantee; add cases instead of a catch-all.

variants.name: Protocol Expression with an interpret method per conformer
variants.idiom_name: protocol Expression declaring interpret(context:) implemented by class or struct nodes
variants.implementation_notes: The object-oriented form: a protocol declaring interpret(context:) with one conformer per grammar rule. It is what you write when nodes are reference types shared across the tree, when a node needs identity, or when the interpreter must accept conformers from other modules; protocol witnesses and existential containers make each call dynamically dispatched, and the closed-set exhaustiveness of the indirect enum is lost.
pitfalls: Existential Expression boxes each node and blocks inlining; use generics or the indirect enum for hot evaluation paths.
A protocol requirement cannot express the closed set, so a missing rule surfaces as a runtime failure in whichever conformer is incomplete.
Class conformers need final or a closed hierarchy to avoid subclass surprises; struct conformers copy large subtrees on assignment.
